approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill updates the Australian Civilian Corps Act 2011 after the aid agency AusAID was abolished and merged into the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
It transfers the powers and duties of the former AusAID head to the DFAT Secretary and replaces all references to AusAID and its director with DFAT and its secretary.
The changes take effect from 1 November 2013, and the bill also updates several subordinate legislative instruments and directions.
Transfers powers and functions from the Director-General of AusAID to the Secretary of DFAT.
Substitutes references to AusAID and its Director-General with DFAT and its Secretary in the Act.
Makes consequential amendments to the Australian Civilian Corps Regulations 2011 and related directions.
The Australian Civilian Corps, the Secretary of DFAT, and staff and operations formerly under AusAID.

Introduced brief remarks on the Australian Civilian Corps Amendment Bill 2013, noting it stems from the government's September announcement to integrate AusAID into the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

Supported the Australian Civilian Corps Amendment Bill 2013 transferring the Corps, which has more than 489 registered specialists across 14 fields, from AusAID to DFAT, but opposed the government's $4½ billion cut to foreign aid and criticised the scrapping of AusAID's graduate program after offers had gone to two or three dozen recruits.

Criticised the government for cancelling the 2014 AusAID graduate program after 35 recruits had already relocated to Canberra, and for leaving 132 non-ongoing DFAT staff and 81 non-ongoing AusAID staff without job certainty amid a $4.5 billion aid budget cut and 12,000 public service job losses.

Supported integrating AusAID into DFAT, noting AusAID spent almost 7 per cent of the aid budget on administration against a 5.2 per cent OECD average, and detailed a $10 million humanitarian package for Typhoon Haiyan including $3 million through non-government organisations and $4 million to the UN flash appeal.

Paid tribute to AusAID, formed in December 1973, citing its work vaccinating more than 2.7 million children last year, building over 4,400 kilometres of road, and giving 33,500 Timorese farmers higher-yielding seeds through the Seeds of Life project, before its dissolution under the government's $4.5 billion aid cut.

Supported the Australian Civilian Corps Amendment Bill 2013, noting the Corps has deployed specialists to 11 countries, and highlighted a $35 million tuberculosis clinic built by the former Labor government in Daru, Papua New Guinea, while opposing the government's $4.5 billion foreign aid cuts and citing domestic violence rates near 85 per cent in the PNG highlands.

Defended integrating AusAID into DFAT effective 1 November 2013, noting Australia will remain the world's eighth largest aid donor at around $5 billion a year, and accused Labor of breaking its promise to reach 0.5 per cent of gross national income in aid by 2015-16, later pushed to 2017-18.
